q: Club Brugge reached their only European Cup final in 1978. Who beat them, and at which ground?
a: Liverpool, at Wembley
note: UEFA match page confirms Liverpool 1-0 Club Brugge at Wembley, 10 May 1978. Reworded: the old premise said first Belgian club in a European Cup final, which is true but sounds wrong at a table that remembers Anderlecht winning the 1976 Cup Winners' Cup.

q: KV Mechelen beat Ajax 1-0 to win the 1988 Cup Winners' Cup. Which Dutchman was their coach?
a: Aad de Mos
note: Final and coach confirmed (Wikipedia 1988 CWC final, Aad de Mos). Cut the claim that it was the last European trophy by a Belgian club, because Mechelen then won the 1988 European Super Cup, which is the subject of another question in this set.

q: The Netherlands women won Euro 2017 on home soil. Which country did they beat 4-2 in the final?
a: Denmark
note: UEFA Women's Euro 2017: Netherlands 4-2 Denmark in the final at De Grolsch Veste, Enschede. Confirmed.

q: The highest scoring match in Eredivisie history ended 9-5 in 1960. Which two clubs played it?
a: Feyenoord and Ajax, with Feyenoord winning
note: Eredivisie records list: Feyenoord-Ajax 9-5, 1960-61, and match reports date it 28 August 1960. Still the highest scoring Eredivisie match.

q: The biggest home win in Eredivisie history is Ajax 12-1 in 1971-72. Who were the victims?
a: Vitesse
note: Superlative was wrong. The records list gives Ajax 12-1 Vitesse as the biggest HOME win, but the biggest win overall is VVV-Venlo 0-13 Ajax in 2020. Narrowed to home win.

q: In October 2007 Afonso Alves scored seven goals in one Eredivisie match for Heerenveen. Who were the opponents, beaten 9-0?
a: Heracles Almelo
note: 7 October 2007, Heerenveen 9-0 Heracles Almelo, Alves scored seven. Confirmed by ESPN and match databases.

q: Which Dutch coach took Trinidad and Tobago to their only World Cup, in 2006?
a: Leo Beenhakker
note: Beenhakker took Trinidad and Tobago to the 2006 World Cup, still their only appearance. Confirmed.

q: PEC Zwolle won the 2014 KNVB Cup, their first trophy in 104 years. What was the score in the final against Ajax?
a: 5-1 to Zwolle
note: nl.wikipedia PEC Zwolle: 5-1 win over Ajax on 20 April 2014, described as the first prize in the club's 104 year history.

q: Tilburg's club renamed itself Willem II in 1898. Who was he?
a: King William II of the Netherlands, who was based in Tilburg and died there
note: Renamed Willem II on 12 January 1898 after King Willem II, who had his headquarters in Tilburg and died there. Confirmed.

q: SC Telstar were founded in 1963 and named after what?
a: The Telstar communications satellite
note: Founded 17 July 1963 from VSV and Stormvogels, named after the Telstar communications satellite. Confirmed.

q: NAC Breda got their name from a 1912 merger. Which two clubs joined up?
a: NOAD and ADVENDO
note: NAC = NOAD ADVENDO Combinatie, the two clubs that merged in 1912. Confirmed on the club's Wikipedia page.

q: Sparta are the oldest professional club in the Netherlands, but which Haarlem club, founded in 1879, is the oldest club of any kind?
a: Koninklijke HFC
note: Koninklijke HFC, founded 15 September 1879, described as the oldest existing club in Dutch football. Sparta (1888) is the oldest professional one. Confirmed.

q: Shirt sponsors were allowed in Dutch football from 1982. Which Japanese cassette tape brand sat on Ajax's shirt until 1991?
a: TDK
note: onetime.nl: shirt sponsorship allowed in the Netherlands from 1 July 1982, TDK on the Ajax shirt 1982 to 1991. Confirmed.

q: In 2020 the KNVB blocked FC Emmen's half a million euro main sponsor on grounds of decency. What did the company sell?
a: Sex toys, the webshop EasyToys
note: KNVB blocked the EasyToys deal in September 2020, reported at 500,000 euro a season. Worth knowing the KNVB later relented, but the block itself is as described.

q: In February 2002 Roda JC won 1-0 away at which Italian giant, and still went out of the UEFA Cup?
a: AC Milan, on penalties at the San Siro
note: 28 February 2002, Roda JC won 1-0 at the San Siro, tie level 1-1, Milan through 3-2 on penalties. Confirmed.

q: Sander Boschker won his only Netherlands cap in 2010, a record for the Dutch team. How old was he?
note: Boschker debuted in 2010 aged 39, the oldest debutant and oldest player for the Netherlands. Confirmed.

q: For thirty years people assumed Johan Cruyff skipped the 1978 World Cup over politics. What did he reveal in 2008 was the real reason?
a: A kidnap attempt on his family in Barcelona, with a gun held to his head
note: Cruyff's 2008 radio interview: armed men held a rifle to his head and tied him and his wife up in front of the children at their Barcelona flat, late 1977. Confirmed.

q: Belgium played the first official international between two independent countries in continental Europe, in 1904. Who were the opponents?
a: France
note: Belgium 3-3 France, 1 May 1904, described as the first official international between independent countries on the European continent. Confirmed.

q: In the 1970s Belgium briefly switched to all white shirts for evening matches, and got a new nickname. What were they called?
a: The White Devils
note: Raymond Goethals switched to all white for evening visibility in the 1970s and the side was temporarily called the White Devils. Confirmed.

q: In 1982 a Belgian club paid Waterschei to lie down in the title decider, a scandal that broke two years later. Which club?
a: Standard Liege
note: Standard Liege paid Waterschei to lose the title decider of 8 May 1982; the scandal broke in February 1984. Confirmed on the French Wikipedia case page.

q: In August 2015 ADO Den Haag's goalkeeper equalised against PSV in the 95th minute with a leaping backheel. Who was he?
a: Martin Hansen
note: 11 August 2015, ADO Den Haag 2-2 PSV, Martin Hansen's 95th minute backheel. Confirmed by contemporary reports.

q: Bjorn Kuipers refereed the Euro 2020 final. What was his day job back in Oldenzaal?
a: Running supermarkets
note: Kuipers refereed the Euro 2020 final at Wembley and owns supermarkets (and a hair studio) in Oldenzaal. Confirmed.

q: Roda JC fans call the team De Koempels. What does that word mean?
a: Mining mates, from the Kerkrade coal pits
note: Koempel is Limburgish for a mineworker, from German Kumpel, and carries the sense of mate. The cited Roda Wikipedia page does not actually explain it, so the source was swapped for one that does.

q: In January 2010 a Dutch professional club founded in 1889 went bankrupt in mid-season and was thrown out of the Eerste Divisie. Which club?
a: HFC Haarlem
note: Bankruptcy 25 January 2010 confirmed by NOS. Killed two claims: the club was 120, not 121 (founded 1889), and no source supports first ever mid-season bankruptcy, only first of four between 2010 and 2013.

q: Which Dutch coach snapped at a journalist with a line that entered the Dutch language, 'Am I so smart, or are you so stupid?'
a: Louis van Gaal
note: Van Gaal to journalist Ted van Leeuwen, 1996. Ensie confirms the wording 'Ben ik nou zo slim of ben jij zo dom?'. The English rendering keeps it intact.

q: Belgian clubs each carry a matricule, a registration number by seniority. Which club is number 1?
a: Royal Antwerp
note: Matricule numbers introduced in 1926 by order of affiliation; Antwerp registered first in 1895 and got number one. Confirmed.

q: Racing Genk were created in 1988 by merging two clubs from the Limburg coalfield. Name either of them.
a: Winterslag or Waterschei Thor
note: KRC Genk formed in 1988 from Waterschei Thor and KFC Winterslag, keeping Winterslag's matricule. Confirmed.

q: Which Kerkrade born coach, who gave his name to a skills training method, won the 1974 UEFA Cup with Feyenoord?
a: Wiel Coerver
note: Coerver born in Kerkrade 3 December 1924, won the 1973-74 UEFA Cup with Feyenoord, gave his name to the Coerver Method. Confirmed.

q: Fed up with the amateur KNVB, ten clubs set up a rebel professional league in 1954. Which two clubs played its first match, on 14 August?
a: Alkmaar '54 and Sportclub Venlo '54
note: nl.wikipedia NBVB: ten clubs, and the Alkmaar '54 v Sportclub Venlo '54 friendly of 14 August 1954 (3-0, about 13,000 in) is treated as the first official NBVB match. Trimmed from 161 characters.

q: The Netherlands' first paid football club was founded in Geleen in June 1954 by a building contractor. What was it called?
a: Fortuna '54
note: nl.wikipedia: Fortuna '54 founded 1 June 1954 in Geleen by contractor Gied Joosten and was immediately the first paid football club in the Netherlands. Confirmed.

q: After the 1953 flood, a team of Dutch professionals playing abroad beat France 2-1 in Paris. What did that match trigger back home?
a: Professional football in the Netherlands
note: 12 March 1953 at the Parc des Princes, France 1-2 Netherlands, De Harder and Appel. nl.wikipedia calls it the direct cause of professional football in the Netherlands. Trimmed from 183 characters.

q: Koninklijke HFC, the oldest club in the Netherlands, was founded in 1879 by Pim Mulier. How old was he at the time?
note: Wikipedia: HFC established 15 September 1879 by the 14 year old Pim Mulier. Confirmed. Flag for the compiler: this overlaps with the extreme row that asks which club is the oldest, so do not use both in one game.

q: Belgium won Olympic gold in 1920 without finishing the final. Why did it stop after 39 minutes?
a: Czechoslovakia walked off in protest at the referee and were disqualified
note: 1920 final abandoned in the 39th minute at 2-0 after Czechoslovakia walked off over the refereeing; they were disqualified and got no silver. Confirmed.

q: The Netherlands took bronze at the 1920 Olympics, but only after losing the medal match itself. Who beat them to silver?
a: Spain
note: Spain won the repechage and then beat the Netherlands 3-1 in the silver and bronze match. Confirmed.

q: Anderlecht overturned a 2-0 deficit in the 1984 UEFA Cup semi-final, then admitted 13 years later they had bribed the referee. Which club went out?
a: Nottingham Forest
note: Forest won the first leg 2-0, Anderlecht the second 3-0, admitted in 1997. Cut the 27,000 pound figure: the cited source itself says 18,000, so the sum is disputed and had no business being in a question. Also trimmed from 176 characters.

q: Standard's players bribed Waterschei to hand them the 1982 Belgian title. What was their stated motive for wanting an easy afternoon?
a: To avoid injuries before the Cup Winners' Cup final against Barcelona days later
note: French Wikipedia case page gives the motive as avoiding injuries before the Cup Winners' Cup final against Barcelona, played four days after the fixed match. Confirmed.

q: KV Mechelen followed their 1988 Cup Winners' Cup with the European Super Cup. Which Dutch side, the European champions, did they beat over two legs?
a: PSV
note: Mechelen beat PSV 3-0 and lost 1-0, 3-1 on aggregate, legs played 1 and 8 February 1989. Trimmed from 157 characters.

q: Which Nigerian scored the first ever goal in the rebranded Champions League, in November 1992, and for which club?
a: Daniel Amokachi, for Club Brugge
note: Amokachi scored on 25 November 1992 in the 16th minute, Club Brugge 1-0 CSKA Moscow. Checked the other three matches that night: the next earliest goal was Boksic on 31 minutes, so the first ever claim holds.

q: Two Brussels clubs, Racing White and Daring, merged in 1973 because nobody was turning up. What did the new club win two seasons later?
a: The Belgian title, in 1974-75, as RWD Molenbeek
note: Racing White and Daring merged in July 1973 over poor attendances and won the 1974-75 Belgian title as RWD Molenbeek. Confirmed.

q: A Belgian club took FIFA to court after their Moroccan midfielder Abdelmajid Oulmers was injured on international duty in 2004. Which club?
a: Sporting Charleroi
note: Oulmers was injured playing for Morocco against Burkina Faso in November 2004 and Charleroi took the case against FIFA. Confirmed.

q: KAA Gent are nicknamed the Buffalos. Where does that come from?
a: Buffalo Bill's Wild West show visiting the city
note: Wikipedia: the Buffalos name comes from Buffalo Bill's Wild West show visiting Ghent in the early 20th century. Confirmed.

q: In 2003 a Belgian club fielded a squad packed with graduates of an Ivorian academy, including Yaya Toure and Emmanuel Eboue. Which club?
a: KSK Beveren
note: Confirmed, but the source was wrong: the JMG Academy page says nothing about Beveren. Swapped to the Beveren page, which names the ASEC Mimosas pipeline and Eboue, Boka, Romaric and Yaya Toure.

q: Where exactly was RSC Anderlecht founded in May 1908?
a: In a cafe, the Concordia, in Anderlecht
note: Founded as Sporting Club Anderlechtois on 27 May 1908 at the Concordia cafe in the Rue d'Aumale. Confirmed.

q: Which Anderlecht great, known as the White Pele, lined up alongside Pele and Bobby Moore in the film Escape to Victory?
a: Paul Van Himst
note: L'Equipe coined le Pele blanc for Van Himst, and he played Michel Fileu in Escape to Victory (1981). Confirmed.

q: Before he was a cyclist, Remco Evenepoel was a midfielder at Anderlecht and PSV. What job did he have in Belgium's youth teams?
a: He was the captain
note: Wikipedia supports captaining Anderlecht and Belgium youth teams, and nine caps at U15 and U16, but does not pin the armband to the U16 side specifically. Widened to youth teams so the claim matches the evidence.

q: The first foreigner to win the Belgian Golden Shoe, in 1975 at RWD Molenbeek, later won three straight titles as Anderlecht coach. Who was he?
a: Johan Boskamp
note: Boskamp won the 1975 Golden Shoe, confirmed as the first foreigner on the roll, and took Anderlecht to the 1993, 1994 and 1995 titles. Trimmed from 160 characters.

q: In September 1965 Go Ahead hosted their first European tie in Deventer and lost 6-0. To whom?
a: Celtic
note: Checked because the Dutch page lists the two legs as 0-1 and 6-0 without saying which was where. English Wikipedia confirms the 6-0 was the first leg at De Adelaarshorst, 29 September 1965.

q: The eagle on the Go Ahead Eagles badge has exactly seven feathers per wing. Why seven?
a: Because seven is a lucky number
note: nl.wikipedia quotes the badge designer that seven is a lucky number, and notes a printing error once gave eight feathers. Confirmed.

q: Jan Jongbloed became the oldest man ever to play in the Eredivisie, aged 44, in 1985. Which club was he keeping goal for?
a: Go Ahead Eagles
note: Eredivisie records list: Jan Jongbloed, Go Ahead Eagles, 44 years 9 months 14 days in 1985, oldest Eredivisie player. Confirmed.

q: Rinus Michels took over a relegation threatened Ajax in January 1965. His first match finished 9-3. Who were the opponents?
a: MVV Maastricht
note: Michels took over in January 1965 and his first match, 24 January 1965, was Ajax 9-3 MVV. Confirmed by the Nationaal Archief photo caption and Ajax's own history pages.

q: MVV players are called De Sterrendragers, the star bearers. Where does the star come from?
a: The five pointed star in the coat of arms of Maastricht
note: nl.wikipedia MVV: Sterrendragers comes from the five pointed star in the Maastricht coat of arms, which is also on the club badge. Confirmed.

q: MVV have played European football exactly once, winning their group in 1970. In which competition?
a: The Intertoto Cup
note: nl.wikipedia MVV: their only European campaign was the 1970 Intertoto Cup, where they won their group. Confirmed.

q: Joop van Daele's goal won Feyenoord the 1970 Intercontinental Cup against Estudiantes. What did the Argentines do to him seconds later?
a: Pulled off his glasses and snapped them in half
note: Rijnmond: Malbernat pulled the glasses off and Pachame snapped them, straight after the goal in the 1970 Intercontinental Cup at De Kuip. Confirmed.

q: Ajax refused to play the 1973 Intercontinental Cup after their bruising 1972 meeting with Independiente. Which club took their place and lost?
a: Juventus
note: Ajax declined, citing the rough treatment from Independiente in 1972 among other reasons; runners-up Juventus played instead and lost 1-0 in Rome. Confirmed.

q: PSV won the 1988 European Cup with a record nobody has matched. What was odd about their run?
a: They won only three matches in the whole campaign, and none from the quarter-finals onwards
note: Checked the superlative: PSV won only three matches in the 1987-88 campaign and none from the quarter-finals on, going through on away goals twice and then penalties. Confirmed.

q: De Kuip opened in 1937 with two free hanging tiers and no pillars. Which two stadiums were the models?
a: Highbury and Yankee Stadium
note: Wikipedia De Kuip: the design drew on Highbury's new double decker stands and Yankee Stadium. Confirmed.

q: De Kuip nearly did not survive the Second World War. What did the German occupiers want to do with it?
a: Dismantle it for scrap metal
note: Wikipedia De Kuip: nearly torn down for scrap by the German occupiers. Confirmed.

q: NAC against Feyenoord in October 1979 was abandoned when a linesman was knocked out by a glass ashtray. How were the last 30 minutes finally played?
a: In an empty stadium, in April 1980
note: Two errors. It was 30 minutes, not 27, replayed on 23 April 1980, and the stadium was empty but over 3,000 fans watched on a screen mounted on a lift truck outside. Also trimmed from 165 characters.

q: The first foreign professional in Dutch football arrived at Heracles in 1957 and was nicknamed the Black Meteor. Who was he?
a: Steve Mokone, from South Africa
note: Wikipedia: Mokone, nicknamed the Black Meteor, played for Heracles 1957-59 and was the first foreign professional in Dutch football. Confirmed.

q: Heracles Almelo had to change their spelling in 1906. What were they called when founded in 1903?
a: Hercules
note: Founded 1903 as Hercules, forced to change in 1906 because a Hercules from Enschede was already in the competition, so they took the Greek form. Confirmed.

q: PEC in PEC Zwolle stands for a combination of two 1910 clubs, one named after a prince and one with a motto. What is that motto?
a: Ende Desespereert Nimmer, never despair
note: nl.wikipedia PEC Zwolle: PEC stands for Prins Hendrik Ende Desespereert Nimmer Combinatie, from the 1910 merger. Confirmed.

q: Dennis Bergkamp's father named him after Denis Law, but the name gained a letter. Why?
a: The Dutch registrar would not accept Denis, so his father added a second n
note: Wikipedia: the extra n was inserted by his father after the registrar would not accept Denis under Dutch naming rules. Confirmed.

q: To prove he had the nerve to drop anyone, Louis van Gaal did something startling in the Bayern Munich dressing room. What?
a: Dropped his trousers
note: Bayern dressing room, early in 2009-10, in front of Luca Toni; Van Bommel and Toni both described the point as him showing he had the stones to drop anyone. Confirmed.

q: In 1975 an amateur club from Spakenburg knocked out three professional sides and reached the KNVB Cup semi-final. Which club?
a: IJsselmeervogels
note: 1974-75 KNVB Cup: IJsselmeervogels beat SC Amersfoort, FC Groningen and AZ '67, then lost 6-0 to Twente in the semi-final. Confirmed.

q: The fastest own goal in Eredivisie history came after nine seconds, in 2006-07. Which club's defender managed it?
a: FC Groningen, through Arnold Kruiswijk
note: Eredivisie records list: Arnold Kruiswijk, FC Groningen, own goal after 9 seconds against Heracles in 2006-07. Confirmed.

q: The fastest goal in Eredivisie history took eight seconds. Koos Waslander did it in 1981-82 for which club?
a: NAC
note: Waslander scored after 8 seconds for NAC against PEC Zwolle on 20 March 1982. The record is now shared with Vito van Crooij (2022), but naming Waslander keeps the answer single.

q: The youngest goalscorer in Eredivisie history was 16 years and 100 days old in 1959-60. Which fishing town club did Wim Kras play for?
a: Volendam
note: Eredivisie records list: Wim Kras, Volendam, 16 years and 100 days, 1959-60. Confirmed.

q: The fastest hat-trick in Eredivisie history took two minutes, scored by Jan Seelen in 1958-59. For which club?
a: Ajax
note: Eredivisie records list: Jan Seelen, Ajax, three goals in two minutes against SHS on 22 March 1959. Confirmed, and he was indeed an Ajax player then.

q: Ruud Gullit was not born with that surname. What was he registered as?
a: Rudi Dil, his mother's surname
note: Wikipedia: registered as Rudi Dil, his mother's surname; he took his father's name at DWS. Confirmed.

q: The 1974 UEFA Cup final at De Kuip was wrecked by rioting in the away end. Which visiting manager took the microphone to call his own fans a disgrace?
a: Bill Nicholson of Tottenham
note: Riot confirmed on the final's Wikipedia page; Nicholson's tannoy line, 'You are a disgrace to Tottenham Hotspur and a disgrace to England', is widely quoted. Trimmed from 174 characters.

q: The FA's founding meetings in 1863 banned hacking, kicking opponents in the shins. Which club walked out in protest and went off towards rugby?
a: Blackheath
note: Wikipedia: Blackheath withdrew at the sixth meeting on 8 December 1863 when hacking was removed, and other carrying-game clubs followed. Trimmed from 161 characters.

q: Herbert Chapman spent years lobbying to get a London Underground station renamed, and won in 1932. Which station?
a: Gillespie Road, which became Arsenal
note: Gillespie Road became Arsenal on 31 October 1932 after months of Chapman lobbying, complete with his 'Whoever heard of Gillespie Road' line. Arsenal's own page 403s to a fetch, but the story is confirmed elsewhere.

q: Juventus gave up their pink shirts in 1903 after a delivery arrived from England. Whose kit did they end up wearing?
a: Notts County's black and white stripes
note: 1903, pink shirts faded, an Englishman at Juventus with Notts County connections had black and white striped shirts sent over from Nottingham. Confirmed.

q: The Daily Mail called Wolves champions of the world after they beat Honved in 1954. What did the annoyed Frenchman Gabriel Hanot launch in response?
a: The European Cup
note: Headline was 'Hail Wolves champions of the world now'; Hanot of L'Equipe used it to push the European club competition. Trimmed twice, from 166 characters.

q: Chievo Verona are known as the Flying Donkeys. Who came up with the name?
a: Hellas Verona fans, who jeered that donkeys would fly before Chievo reached Serie A
note: Wikipedia: the taunt was a Hellas Verona chant, donkeys will fly before Chievo are in Serie A, which Chievo fans took over after promotion in 2001. Confirmed.

q: Which change to the Football League did Jimmy Hill campaign for, adopted in England in 1981?
a: Three points for a win instead of two
note: Wikipedia: three points for a win was proposed by Jimmy Hill and introduced in England in 1981. Confirmed.

q: Which law arrived for the 1992-93 season, blamed largely on how dull the 1990 World Cup had been?
a: The back-pass rule, keepers could no longer pick up a deliberate kick from a team mate
note: Adopted by FIFA in May 1992 after the 1990 World Cup was widely criticised as dull and full of back-passing. Confirmed.

q: A riot at Dinamo Zagreb's ground in May 1990 turned their 21 year old captain into a Croatian national symbol. Who was he and what did he do?
a: Zvonimir Boban, who kicked a policeman who was beating a Dinamo fan
note: 13 May 1990 at Maksimir. Wikipedia: Dinamo captain Boban kicked policeman Refik Ahmetovic, who was mistreating a Dinamo fan. Boban was born 8 October 1968, so 21. Confirmed.

q: Serbia against Albania in Belgrade in 2014 was abandoned after an object appeared over the pitch. What was it?
a: A drone trailing a Greater Albania flag
note: 14 October 2014 in Belgrade, abandoned when a drone flew a Greater Albania banner over the pitch and Mitrovic pulled it down. Confirmed.

q: Alcohol was banned in Scottish football grounds after trouble at which 1980 match?
a: The Scottish Cup final between Celtic and Rangers, which ended in a mass brawl on the Hampden pitch
note: 1980 Scottish Cup final, Celtic 1-0 Rangers, running battle on the Hampden pitch blamed on drink; Parliament then banned alcohol at Scottish grounds. Confirmed.

q: Saint-Étienne fans still blame one feature of Hampden Park for the 1976 European Cup final. What?
a: The square goalposts, two of their efforts came back off the crossbar
note: Checked the two efforts claim: Wikipedia's final report has Bathenay's shot off the bar on 34 minutes and Santini's header off the bar shortly after, hence les poteaux carres. Confirmed.

q: Brian Clough called Poland's goalkeeper a circus clown in gloves before the 1973 Wembley qualifier. What did the 1-1 draw cost England?
a: Their place at the 1974 World Cup
note: Checked the quote, since a shortened 'a clown' version also circulates. The fuller 'circus clown in gloves' is the reported wording, and the 1-1 draw on 17 October 1973 cost England the 1974 World Cup. Confirmed.

q: 1. FC Köln's mascot is a live goat called Hennes. Who was he named after?
a: Hennes Weisweiler, the club's player-coach when a circus gave them the goat in 1950
note: Club's own page: the Williams Circus handed over the goat on 13 February 1950 and it was named for player-coach Hennes Weisweiler. Confirmed.

q: Which Italian club was founded by an Englishman from Nottingham who said their colours would be red like fire and black like the fear they caused?
a: AC Milan, founded by Herbert Kilpin
note: Milan and Kilpin of Nottingham are solid, but the cited Wikipedia page carries no such quote and the line survives in several wordings (devils, fire, fear). Source swapped to one that carries it, and the question paraphrases rather than quotes.

q: AS Roma were created in 1927 by merging clubs from the city. Which Rome club refused to be part of it?
a: Lazio
note: 1927 merger of Roman, Alba-Audace and Fortitudo; Lazio was the one major Roman club that refused. Confirmed.

q: Wales and Juventus forward John Charles played more than 700 games. What did he never once receive?
a: A booking or a sending off
note: Football365 confirms he was never booked or sent off. The old wording, 'what never once happened to him', had no single defensible answer, so it now asks what he never received.

q: Germans call miserable rainy weather Fritz Walter weather after the 1954 World Cup winning captain. Why did he play better in it?
a: Malaria he caught as a prisoner of war left him unable to handle heat
note: Wikipedia: Walter caught malaria as a prisoner of war and struggled in heat, so wet heavy conditions suited him. Confirmed.

q: How did Galatasaray fans greet Manchester United at Istanbul airport in 1993?
a: Banners reading Welcome to Hell
note: Irish Times: United were met at Istanbul airport in 1993 by the infamous Welcome to Hell banner. Confirmed.

q: After Scotland beat England 2-1 at Wembley in 1977, what did their fans take home with them?
a: The goalposts, which they snapped, and lumps of the pitch
note: 4 June 1977, Scotland 2-1 at Wembley, McQueen and Dalglish; fans tore down the goalposts and dug up pieces of the pitch. Confirmed.

q: The first football match under floodlights was played in 1878, before Edison had even patented his light bulb. At which ground?
a: Bramall Lane in Sheffield
note: 14 October 1878 at Bramall Lane, lit by four 30 foot lamps on wooden towers. Edison's bulb patent came in January 1880, so the framing holds. Confirmed.

q: The European Championship trophy is named after the Frenchman who pushed for the tournament from the 1920s. What did he never get to see?
a: The tournament itself, Henri Delaunay died in 1955 and the first Euros were in 1960
note: Delaunay proposed the idea in 1927, died 9 November 1955, first Euros 1960, trophy named after him. Confirmed.

q: Italy's oldest club was founded in 1893 at the British consulate and still spells its name the English way. Which club?
a: Genoa, rather than Genova
note: Genoa Cricket and Athletic Club founded 7 September 1893 at the British consulate, Italy's oldest surviving club, and it kept the English spelling. Confirmed.

q: AEK Athens were founded in 1924 by refugees from one city, and their badge still says so. Which city?
a: Constantinople, hence the Byzantine double-headed eagle
note: AEK founded 13 April 1924 by Constantinopolitan refugees, hence the double-headed eagle. Confirmed.

q: The original FA Cup was stolen from a Birmingham shop window in 1895 and never recovered. Which club had just won it?
a: Aston Villa, who were fined 25 pounds to replace it
note: Stolen overnight on 11-12 September 1895 from William Shillcock's shop window in Birmingham, never recovered; Villa had won it that April and were fined 25 pounds. Confirmed.

q: In April 1938 Austria played Germany in Vienna in a match staged to celebrate the Anschluss, and a polite draw was expected. What happened?
a: Austria won 2-0, Sindelar scoring the first
note: 3 April 1938 at the Prater, Austria 2-0, Sindelar and Sesta scoring late. Cut the celebration in front of the Nazi dignitaries from the answer: Wikipedia carries it only as an unattributed claim, so it is folklore, not a fact to award points on.

q: Borussia Mönchengladbach beat Inter 7-1 in the 1971 European Cup and still went out. Why?
a: UEFA annulled the game after Roberto Boninsegna was hit by a can of Coca-Cola, and the replay finished 0-0
note: Inter's own account: 7-1 on 20 October 1971 annulled after Boninsegna was hit by a Coca-Cola can, Inter won the San Siro leg 4-2 and the Berlin replay finished 0-0. Confirmed.

q: Wales reached the 1958 World Cup without winning their qualifying group. How did they get in?
a: Their name came out of a hat for a play-off against Israel, whose scheduled opponents had all refused to play them
note: Wales came out of a second draw of lots in December 1957 after Belgium declined; Israel had reached that stage without playing, as Turkey, Indonesia and Sudan all withdrew or refused. Confirmed.

q: Hertha BSC took their name in 1892 from something the founder had been on with his father. What?
a: A steamship called Hertha, whose blue and white funnel also gave them their colours
note: Wikipedia: named after the steamship Hertha, with its blue and white funnel, on which a founder had been out with his father. Confirmed.

q: Facing a refused licence in 2004, Union Berlin fans ran a campaign called Bluten für Union. What did it involve?
a: Donating blood and handing the club the money they were paid for it
note: Club's own page: fans gave blood and handed the expense payment to the club, to help raise the 1.46 million euro guarantee the DFB demanded by 9 June 2004. Confirmed.

q: In 1919 Arsenal were voted into the enlarged First Division without having earned promotion. Which relegated club lost its place to them?
a: Tottenham Hotspur
note: The old answer, fifth in the Second Division, is disputed: the cited Sky piece says sixth, Wikipedia's 1914-15 table says fifth on goal average. Two defensible answers is no good at 20 points, so the question now turns on Tottenham. Also trimmed from 155 characters.

q: Seven players were banned for life over a fixed Good Friday match in 1915. Which two clubs did they come from?
a: Manchester United and Liverpool, who had backed a 2-0 United win at 7-1
note: Good Friday, 2 April 1915, Manchester United 2-0 Liverpool, money laid at 7/1 on that exact score, seven players banned for life. Confirmed.

q: On Christmas Day 1937 Charlton's Sam Bartram was still guarding his goal at Stamford Bridge when a policeman found him. Why?
a: Fog, the match had been abandoned a quarter of an hour earlier and nobody had told him
note: Retiered from BALL to extreme. Fact confirmed: Christmas Day 1937 at Stamford Bridge, abandoned on 61 minutes at 1-1, Bartram left about fifteen minutes until a policeman fetched him, and Snopes rates it true against 1937 press reports. But the answer is essentially 'fog', and this is one of the most retold stories in the game, so it is not a 20 point deep cut.

q: Which East German international defected in 1979 on a trip to Kaiserslautern and died in a 1983 car crash, watched all along by the Stasi?
a: Lutz Eigendorf, of Dynamo Berlin
note: Wikipedia: fled the BFC Dynamo party in West Germany on 20 March 1979, crashed on 5 March 1983 and died two days later, with Stasi surveillance of him and his ex-wife documented. Trimmed from 153 characters.

q: FC St. Pauli's skull and crossbones started with one fan in the 1980s. What did he do?
a: Nailed a Jolly Roger to a broomstick and waved it at the Millerntor, he went by Doc Mabuse
note: St Pauli museum: around 1986 a Hafenstrasse squatter known as Doc Mabuse nailed a Jolly Roger from the Hamburger Dom fair to a broomstick and took it to the Millerntor. Confirmed.

q: French law now bans professional football on one date every year. Which date, and why?
a: 5 May, the anniversary of the 1992 Furiani stand collapse at Bastia
note: Law adopted in February 2020 freezing professional football on 5 May, for the 1992 Furiani stand collapse at Bastia that killed 18 and injured more than 2,300. Confirmed.

q: Spartak Moscow's founder was sent to the gulag in 1942. Which secret police chief, who also ran rivals Dynamo, is blamed for it?
a: Lavrentiy Beria, the man he jailed was Nikolai Starostin
note: Starostin was arrested on 20 March 1942 and sentenced to ten years in Siberia. Beria headed the secret police and was Dynamo president, but the published sentence cited embezzlement, so the question now says blamed rather than stating he put him there.

q: At least 66 people died in a crush at Spartak Moscow's UEFA Cup tie in 1982. When was the death toll finally admitted publicly?
a: 1989, seven years later
note: 20 October 1982, Spartak v HFC Haarlem; the true toll of 66 was only published in July 1989, in Izvestia. Confirmed.

q: Berwick Rangers knocked Rangers out of the Scottish Cup in 1967. What happened to the Rangers forwards Jim Forrest and George McLean?
a: They were blamed for it and never played for Rangers again
note: Wikipedia: Forrest and McLean were made scapegoats, never played for Rangers again and were sold to Preston and Dundee within weeks. Confirmed.

q: Manchester City were drawing 2-2 with Liverpool on the last day of 1995-96 when Alan Ball said a draw would do. Who ran out to say it would not?
a: Niall Quinn, who had been substituted and had heard the real scores
note: Story confirmed, but the detail drifted: the cited account has Quinn picking up the Wimbledon result off BBC radio while being treated, not seeing it on a television. Also trimmed from 175 characters.

q: Manchester United's heaviest defeat, 11-3 in a 1904 friendly, came against an amateur side whose own rules banned them from entering cups. Which side?
a: Corinthian
note: Wikipedia calls it United's heaviest defeat, in a friendly at Leyton in 1904, and confirms Corinthian's constitution barred them from competing for any cup. Added 'friendly' so nobody at the table argues the record is 0-7.

q: Günter Netzer started the 1973 German Cup final on the bench for Borussia Mönchengladbach. How did he end up winning it?
a: He put himself on as a substitute, then scored the winner in extra time
note: Wikipedia: Netzer told Weisweiler he was coming on for Kulik, then scored in the 94th minute with his second touch. Confirmed.

q: Marseille were stripped of the 1993 French title over the Valenciennes bribery case. Who got it instead?
a: Nobody, Paris Saint-Germain were offered it and refused, so the title was left vacant
note: Wikipedia: the LFP allotted the title to PSG, Canal+ refused it, and the 1993 championship was left unattributed. Confirmed.

q: England beat Italy 3-2 in the brutal 1934 Battle of Highbury. What record did the England line-up set that day?
a: Seven of the eleven were Arsenal players
note: 14 November 1934, England 3-2, and Wikipedia confirms it is the only time seven players from one club started for England. Confirmed.

q: Offside was changed in 1925 from three defenders to two, largely to stop one Newcastle full-back. Who?
a: Bill McCracken
note: Wikipedia: McCracken's offside ploy at Newcastle was so effective the law was changed to two defenders in 1925. Confirmed.

q: The corner kick did not come from London. Which city's football association adopted it first, in 1868?
a: Sheffield, after a proposal by Sheffield Norfolk FC
note: Sheffield Home of Football: proposed by Sheffield Norfolk FC and adopted by the Sheffield FA in October 1868. Confirmed.

q: Timo Konietzka scored the first goal in Bundesliga history in 1963, inside the first minute. Why is there almost no record of it?
a: There were no TV cameras there and the photographers were all behind the other goal, expecting Werder Bremen to score
note: Bundesliga.com quotes Konietzka: no TV cameras in the ground at all, and the photographers were behind the other goal expecting Bremen to score. Confirmed.

q: Who scored ten goals in a single match for Germany in 1912 and then had to flee the country in 1937?
a: Gottfried Fuchs, in a 16-0 win over Russia at the Olympics
note: Ten goals in Germany 16-0 Russia at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics, and he left Germany in 1937 because he was Jewish. Confirmed.

q: Thirty three people were crushed to death at Bolton's Burnden Park in 1946. What was done about the match?
a: It was played to the finish, and ended goalless
note: 9 March 1946, 33 dead in the FA Cup tie against Stoke, the match played to a finish and ending goalless. Confirmed.

q: Chris Kirkland's father put a bet on with William Hill at 100-1 when Chris was a boy, and collected nearly 10,000 pounds in 2006. What was the bet?
a: That his son would play for England
note: Two embroidered details cut. The stake was 98.10 pounds, not a round 100, and reports say the bet was laid when Chris was a teenager about ten years earlier, not specifically at 14. The payout, 9,908.10 pounds after his England debut against Greece in August 2006, is solid.

q: Europe had an international club competition from 1927, decades before the European Cup. What was it called?
a: The Mitropa Cup, Hugo Meisl's idea
note: Wikipedia: agreed at a meeting in Venice in July 1927 on Hugo Meisl's initiative, first matches 14 August 1927, with clubs from Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. Confirmed.

q: The 1909 Scottish Cup was never awarded to anyone. What went wrong?
a: The Old Firm final and its replay were both drawn, fans rioted when there was no extra time, and the clubs refused a second replay
note: Final 2-2 and replay 1-1, no extra time under the rules, pitch invasion and goalposts torn down, both clubs asked for the second replay to be scrapped and the trophy was withheld. Confirmed.

q: After liquidation in 2012, the new Rangers company was rejected by the Scottish Premier League. Where did they have to start again?
a: The Third Division, the bottom tier, on a 25-5 vote of the league's clubs
note: Retiered from BALL to extreme. Confirmed: SFL clubs voted 25-5 on 13 July 2012 to put the newco in the Third Division, after SPL clubs had voted 10-2 against. But anyone who follows the game remembers Rangers starting again in the bottom tier, so it is not worth 20.

q: Fourteen players were arrested over Italy's 1980 Totonero betting scandal. What made the arrests so public?
a: They were taken in at the grounds on a live Serie A matchday, some straight off the pitch
note: 23 March 1980, fourteen players taken in at grounds during a live Serie A and B matchday. Confirmed.

q: Who is the pipe-smoking sailor on Sampdoria's shirt?
a: Baciccia, the Genoese form of Giovanni Battista
note: Wikipedia: the sailor is Baciccia, a diminutive of the Ligurian Gio-Batta, that is Giovanni Battista. Confirmed.

q: The goalkeeper who saved four penalties in the 1986 European Cup final shootout never played for Steaua again. Why not?
a: A blood clot in his arm that summer ended his top-level career
note: Duckadam saved all four Barcelona penalties in 1986, then a blood clot blocking the circulation in his arm needed an operation and ended his top-level career at 27. Confirmed.

q: The Intertoto Cup was set up in 1961 to serve an industry rather than the supporters. Which industry?
a: The football pools, so betting coupons had fixtures through the summer
note: Wikipedia: founded 1961-62 by Thommen, Persson and Rappan, named after Toto, the German word for the pools, to keep coupons supplied through the summer. Confirmed.

q: Accrington Stanley resigned from the Football League in March 1962 with 13 matches still to play, then changed their minds. How quickly?
a: Three days later, but the League held them to the first letter
note: Resigned 6 March 1962 with thirteen matches left, president wrote three days later asking the League to ignore it, and the Management Committee accepted the first letter on 11 March. The cited Wikipedia page has the dates; the retraction is confirmed in other accounts.

q: Bohemians Prague are nicknamed the Kangaroos and carry one on the badge. Why?
a: They were given two live kangaroos after touring Australia in 1927, and handed them to Prague Zoo
note: Wikipedia: after the 1927 Australia tour the club was given two live kangaroos and handed them to Prague Zoo, hence the badge and the Klokani nickname. Confirmed.

q: France's oldest club plays in sky blue and navy, the colours of two English universities. Which club, and which universities?
a: Le Havre, in the colours of Oxford and Cambridge
note: Le Havre's English founders split the difference between Cambridge light blue and Oxford dark blue, adopting the halves in 1891. Trimmed from 152 characters.

q: In September 1946 England played two different sides both called Ireland within three days. What did Johnny Carey and Bill Gorman manage?
a: They played for both of them
note: 28 September 1946 at Windsor Park for the IFA XI, 30 September at Dalymount Park for the FAI XI, both against England. Confirmed.
